extracted.intended_audience: disability activists, disability policy/regulation watchers, broadcasters, and the general public interested in disability rights and media ethics
extracted.subtask_description: News coverage of a broadcasting controversy where a comedian's jokes about a disabled child prompted complaints, regulatory investigation, and debate about editorial judgment, discrimination, and hate speech. The piece summarizes stakeholder reactions and regulatory/procedural consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breach of OFCOM's broadcasting code
rubrics_metrics.description: OFCOM launched an investigation after receiving complaints; if found guilty of a breach of OFCOM’s broadcasting code, Channel 4 could face a heavy fine or be forced to broadcast an apology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complaints to OFCOM can trigger formal investigations; possible sanctions include fines or mandated apologies. The page notes OFCOM received a complaint from Katie Price's lawyers and 'a number of other' people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouraging disability hate crimes / causing harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Campaigners say Boyle’s jokes 'would encourage disability hate crimes such as bullying and harassment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate content for likely social harm: whether jokes fuel bullying, harassment or hate crimes against disabled people. Stakeholders (e.g., Jaspal Dhani) cite potential real-world consequences as part of assessing wrongdoing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breaching the UN disability convention
rubrics_metrics.description: Leading disabled activists accused Channel 4 of breaching the UN disability convention by referring to disabled people as 'freaks of nature' in promotional material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess broadcast content and promotions against obligations under international human-rights instruments (UN disability convention) when determining discriminatory treatment or institutional breaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire versus targeted abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Channel 4 defended Boyle by calling the material 'satirical' and 'aimed not at Harvey Price but at "media hypocrisy and celebrity culture"' while critics say the jokes were aimed at Price’s son and were abusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish whether offensive material is legitimate satire critiquing institutions/figures or whether it targets a protected individual/group; intent, target, and context matter when judging acceptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial process and editorial judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Channel 4's disability executive said the jokes had 'gone through an editorial process' and that she was 'prepared to defend' the material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether material passed appropriate editorial review and whether that process adequately considered discrimination, harm, and legal/regulatory risks. Presence of an editorial process is offered as a defense but not conclusive proof of appropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of standards across protected characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics note 'You wouldn't hear that kind of argument being applied to a comedian who used derogatory terms around race. It would not be tolerated,' arguing disability should receive the same protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether broadcasters apply consistent standards for content concerning disability as they do for race, sexuality, etc.; inconsistent application can indicate discrimination or bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pushing boundaries versus going beyond boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Channel 4 framed Boyle as 'a master of saying the unsayable' who 'takes it right to the line and then steps over it,' while critics counter: 'It's not pushing the boundaries, it's going beyond the boundaries.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing provocative comedy, weigh whether material legitimately pushes social or artistic boundaries or whether it exceeds acceptable limits into gratuitous abuse. This is a qualitative judgment invoked by both defenders and critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm to individual, especially a child / bullying a child
rubrics_metrics.description: Katie Price stated Boyle was 'bullying her son,' and her lawyers said Channel 4 was being discriminatory by allowing attacks on her disabled child.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess ethical and legal implications of public commentary about identifiable individuals, particularly children and vulnerable persons; consider child protection, privacy, and additional safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of offensive, disablist language in promotional materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Earlier incidents included a trailer for a Paralympics documentary that referred to disabled people as 'freaks of nature', which activists said breached standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promotional content and trailers should avoid demeaning language; such usage may be treated as evidence of institutional insensitivity or discrimination and attract regulatory/activist response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referral to Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) and inquiry processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Price also complained to the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC), and the incident will be discussed at an EHRC consultation on disability-related harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serious complaints may be escalated to equality/human-rights bodies and become part of formal inquiries or consultations; consider these procedural avenues when evaluating institutional responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcaster credibility and track record on disability coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Channel 4 argued it won the right to broadcast the Paralympics because of its 'brilliant and bold treatment of disability' and willingness to 'take some risks.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess institutional credibility and historical record on disability representation when judging whether a controversial piece reflects an acceptable editorial stance or systemic problems.
